g.text: What a longer task demands of each step

path.style: fill: none; stroke: #2563eb; stroke-width: 2; stroke-linecap: square

text.style: font-size: 9px; font-family: 'Segoe UI', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: start; fill: #0f172a

path.style: fill: none; stroke: #7c3aed; stroke-width: 2; stroke-linecap: square

path.style: fill: none; stroke: #dc2626; stroke-width: 2; stroke-linecap: square

text.style: font-size: 9px; font-family: 'Segoe UI', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: start; fill: #0f172a
font-size: 9.5px; font-family: 'Segoe UI', 'DejaVu Sans'; fill: #475569

g.text: The arithmetic that makes long-horizon agents hard, assuming steps fail independently. A 99%-reliable step -- which sounds

text.style: font-size: 9.5px; font-family: 'Segoe UI', 'DejaVu Sans'; fill: #475569

g.text: excellent -- is a coin flip by step 70 and near-hopeless by step 200. Right: to finish a 100-step task nine times out of ten,

text.style: font-size: 9.5px; font-family: 'Segoe UI', 'DejaVu Sans'; fill: #475569

g.text: every step needs an error budget near 0.1%. This is why the useful work is recovery rather than accuracy: checkpointing,

text.style: font-size: 9.5px; font-family: 'Segoe UI', 'DejaVu Sans'; fill: #475569

g.text: verification, and retry break the chain into segments so a single bad step costs one segment instead of the run. Real steps

text.style: font-size: 9.5px; font-family: 'Segoe UI', 'DejaVu Sans'; fill: #475569

g.text: are not independent -- errors correlate, and a model that recovers turns some failures into successes -- so treat these as

text.style: font-size: 9.5px; font-family: 'Segoe UI', 'DejaVu Sans'; fill: #475569

g.text: the pessimistic bound that motivates the engineering, not a prediction.
